claims.text: The marketing mix is the blend of four controllable elements - product, price, place and promotion - with which a business influences the customers, actual and potential, for what it sells.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Each element reaches the consumer through a different mechanism: the product through fitness for the buyer's need, the price through what the buyer is willing and able to pay, the place through how easily the buyer can get the product, and the promotion through whether the buyer notices the product and knows what it offers.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Which element matters most differs with circumstances: the element that most influences consumer decisions is the one whose weakness would break the purchase, so an unfamiliar new product tends to depend on promotion, while a known convenience product tends to turn on place and price.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The roles of marketing and the elements of the marketing mix are different ideas: the roles are what marketing does for the business, such as identifying customer needs and raising awareness of the product, while the elements are the controllable decisions blended in the mix; listing the elements is not an answer about the roles.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A marketing strategy is a business’s plan for using the elements of the marketing mix together to reach a chosen target market and achieve its marketing objectives.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A justified recommendation of a marketing strategy names the chosen strategy, the circumstances that make it fit - such as the target market, the competition and the business’s objectives - and the criterion that decides between it and the alternatives.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A sound justification also faces the case against: the alternative strategy that might have been chosen, and the conditions under which the recommendation would change.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: The strategy that fits tends to follow the facts of the situation: a niche market with distinctive tastes rewards a differentiated product and selective outlets, while a broad mass market rewards wide availability and a competitive price.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Legal controls on marketing are laws that restrict what businesses may claim in their promotion and require the goods they sell to be safe, of acceptable quality and as described.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Controls on misleading promotion forbid claims that deceive consumers about price, quality or performance: a business that oversteps risks penalties and the forced withdrawal of its promotion, and the lost consumer trust often outlasts the fine, so promotion strategy has to be planned around what can honestly be claimed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Controls on faulty and dangerous goods make product safety part of marketing strategy: testing and compliance raise a business’s costs, but they protect consumers from harm, and a business that can show its products meet the safety standards may turn that record into a selling point.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Legal controls reshape marketing strategy rather than end it: honest claims take the place of exaggerated ones, product design budgets for safety testing, and price comparisons have to be truthful, so the business adapts its marketing within the rules.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A foreign market is the group of customers, actual and potential, for a product in a country other than the business’s own; entering it means beginning to sell to customers in that country.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: New markets in other countries offer growth potential because they add customers beyond the home market’s existing demand: sales that have stopped growing at home may still grow abroad, and selling in several countries can reduce a business’s dependence on any single economy.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: How much growth a foreign market offers depends on its facts: how many potential customers it holds, what they can afford and are willing to pay, how strong the local competitors are, and how well the product fits what consumers there prefer.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Cultural differences - in language, tastes, religious customs and buying habits - can make a sound product or its promotion misunderstood or unwelcome abroad, so a business that enters without adapting may lose sales it assumed it would win.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Lack of knowledge about a foreign market - its laws, its competitors, its distribution channels and its consumers’ preferences - raises the cost and the risk of entering, because the business cannot price, place or promote confidently while it is working from assumptions.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Distance brings its own problems: transport and communication costs tend to run higher on foreign sales, and a change in currency values between agreeing a sale and receiving payment can shrink the N$ the business finally banks.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A joint venture is a shared enterprise in which two or more businesses agree to set up and jointly own a new business, each contributing investment and sharing the risks and the profits.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Licensing is an agreement in which the owner of a product grants a producer in another country the right to make and sell that product there, in return for payments - usually a royalty on the sales made.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: A joint venture and a licensing agreement trade control against risk: a joint venture keeps the business part-owner, sharing costs and risk with a partner who knows the local market, while licensing needs little investment and reaches the market quickly but leaves quality, pricing and the brand’s reputation in the licensee’s hands.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.

claims.text: Which method fits depends on the circumstances: how much control the business wants to keep, how much investment and risk it can carry, how quickly it needs to be selling, and how much local knowledge the product needs to succeed.

verification.method: Authored originally against the 0450 v2 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft. Requires independent semantic review (RS-28) before publication.
